title: Robodebt
subtitle: When the formula says you owe us

overall.label: Institutional failure + misconduct
overall.summary: The strongest evidence supports a system that raised debts using an invalid averaging method, persisted despite serious legal and accuracy warnings, and later concealed or misstated important problems. The evidence examined so far does not require a secret cabal to explain what happened.

claims.claim: Debts raised solely from averaged ATO income, without evidence of constant fortnightly earnings, were not validly made under the legal pathway used.
claims.why: Federal Court proceedings, later declarations and the Commonwealth's withdrawal of averaging-based debts converge on this point.

claims.claim: Responsible agencies continued the scheme after substantial legal, fairness and accuracy warnings should have forced reconsideration.
claims.why: The developing chronology includes 2014 legal concerns, a 2015 legislative-change issue and strong Royal Commission findings about the 2017 period.

claims.claim: Public and parliamentary explanations overstated the scheme's legality or accuracy beyond what the underlying record justified.
claims.why: This remains open pending a systematic Hansard and statement-by-statement comparison.

claims.claim: The dominant explanation is policy incentives, automation, weak legal gatekeeping and diffusion of responsibility rather than a single secret plan to invent unlawful debts.
claims.why: Current material strongly supports systemic failure and misconduct but has not produced positive evidence of a top-level conspiracy to create debts known to be unlawful.

timeline.event: Income averaging is proposed. DSS legal concerns include that annual smoothing or averaging may not be consistent with the legislative framework. DHS analysis reportedly finds a very high mismatch between averaged and manual calculations.
timeline.effect: Early legal and accuracy red flags

timeline.event: DSS considers legislative change necessary. The proposal proceeds through the executive process and an Executive Minute is signed on 20/02/2015.
timeline.effect: Raises the process question: what exactly reached decision-makers?

timeline.event: The Royal Commission later finds the scheme should by then have been abandoned or radically revised. It also identifies serious failures in dealings with the Ombudsman, including withholding earlier legal advice.
timeline.effect: Strongly shifts C2 toward persistence and misconduct

timeline.event: Amato litigation becomes a clean legal turning point: averaged ATO income alone could not establish the asserted debt in the way used.
timeline.effect: Strong object-level evidence against the averaging method

timeline.event: Prygodicz settlement approval records the withdrawal of a very large class of averaging-based debts. The judgment also cautions against simplistic claims that senior actors all had actual knowledge from the beginning.
timeline.effect: Confirms scale while constraining overclaiming about intent

timeline.event: The Royal Commission characterises Robodebt as a costly failure of public administration and makes detailed findings about legality, fairness, advice and institutional conduct.
timeline.effect: Strong support for institutional failure + misconduct

hypotheses.title: Good-faith lawful shortcut
hypotheses.text: Averaging was a lawful and reasonable shortcut, errors were incidental, and the system was corrected when problems emerged.
hypotheses.test: This predicts supportive legal advice, tolerable error rates and rapid correction after serious warnings. The evidence examined so far fits poorly.

hypotheses.title: System failure + incentives
hypotheses.text: A defective administrative model was reinforced by fiscal targets, automation, weak legal gatekeeping, bureaucracy and diffusion of responsibility.
hypotheses.test: This predicts messy advice, ignored red flags, persistence and defensive institutional behaviour without requiring a secret command structure. Current evidence fits strongly.

hypotheses.title: Senior misconduct
hypotheses.text: Some senior actors ignored, buried or misrepresented serious legal risk after it became apparent.
hypotheses.test: This requires dated evidence tying named decision-makers to warnings, concealment or misleading representations. The 2017 chronology provides material support, but actor-by-actor findings must remain precise.

hypotheses.title: Secret cabal to invent debts
hypotheses.text: A small group secretly coordinated to create debts they knew were unlawful from the outset.
hypotheses.test: This requires positive evidence of coordination and intent. None of the material examined so far earns that conclusion.

openQuestions: Complete page-level verification against the full Royal Commission report and primary exhibits.
Build the dated legal-advice matrix from original documents rather than summaries alone.
Audit Hansard and ministerial statements for C3: legality, accuracy and representations to Parliament or the public.
Keep actual knowledge, constructive knowledge, negligence and deliberate concealment separate for each actor.
Test the causal model against evidence that could support a more centrally directed explanation.
wouldChange: Primary legal material showing the averaging method was lawful in the form actually used would materially weaken C1.
Evidence that the scheme was stopped promptly on receipt of the first serious legal warning would weaken C2.
Direct documentary evidence that senior actors ordered continuation because they knew debts were unlawful would materially strengthen the intentional-coordination hypothesis.
A systematic Hansard audit showing careful, qualified public explanations would weaken C3.
